617.title: As on a mountain
617.hook: live as if on a mountain; here or there matters little (Meditations 10.15)
617.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use the mountain as a mental vantage point: in the middle of daily friction they picture the wide view, and try to act as they would from there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus on getting to know change. Your line was study change. What did you see changing, when you really looked? Day six hundred seventeen.

People dream of the cabin. The mountain view, the quiet, the place where you'll finally be the calm, wise version of yourself. Back in book four, Marcus noted that people seek retreats in the country, by the sea, in the hills, and said you can retreat into yourself instead. In book ten he comes at the same idea from the other side, with a short, strong instruction. Today: as on a mountain.
screen: `THE CABIN DREAM.` → `RETREAT INTO YOURSELF.` → `AS ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the line, in George Long's 1862 translation: “Short is the little which remains to thee of life. Live as on a mountain.” Second, what the mountain means. It makes no difference, Marcus goes on, whether a person lives here or there, as long as they live everywhere in the world as a citizen of one great city. The mountain isn't a place you move to. It's a way of standing: above the noise, seeing far, not tangled in every small quarrel of the town below. Third, living in plain view. Let people see, he says, let them know, a real human being living by nature. And then a hard line: if they can't stand him, let them kill him, because that's better than living the way they live. It's the voice of a man who knew public life could be dangerous, and who wanted to be the same in public as in private. Fourth, why the mountain and not the cabin. The cabin promises you'll be different somewhere else. Marcus says the shortness of life means there's no time to wait for the right setting. The height has to come with you, into the office, the kitchen, the commute. Here or there matters little. What you carry matters a great deal.
screen: `LIFE IS SHORT; LIVE AS ON A MOUNTAIN.` · `HERE OR THERE MATTERS LITTLE.` · `LIVE IN PLAIN VIEW.` · `BRING THE HEIGHT WITH YOU.` · then, large: `AS ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit somewhere high or quiet: a top step, a window, a balcony, a hill, or just a corner where the noise drops. Otherwise, close your eyes and picture a mountain ledge. Breathe in the height. From up here, look down at today's small tangles: the email, the argument, the errand. See how small and far away they look. Then remember that you'll carry this view back down with you. The bell holds the time.
George Long, whose translation gives Marcus's instruction: short is the little that remains of life, so live as on a mountain. Today's word.
Your line: here or there matters little. Once today, in the middle of something small and tangled, step up a level in your mind and look down at it. Day six hundred seventeen.

618.title: Is it this you'd miss?
618.hook: afraid of death? is it this particular errand you'd miss? (Meditations 10.29)
618.tomorrow: Let no one say it truly
618.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations pause during routine tasks and ask Marcus's question, which helps them see trivial worries at their real size and notice which parts of the day they truly value.

segments.voice: Yesterday: as on a mountain. Your line was here or there matters little. Did you get a view from up there, in the middle of something tangled? Day six hundred eighteen.

You're refolding towels. Answering the fourteenth email about the same meeting. Scrolling past a video you've already seen three times. Then someone leans in and asks: if you had to leave this life today, is this what you'd miss? It's an odd question to ask over a basket of laundry, and an odd one to ask yourself at all. But Marcus asks it in book ten, and he asks it of everything he does. Today: second edge.
screen: `REFOLDING TOWELS.` → `THE FOURTEENTH EMAIL.` → `IS IT THIS YOU'D MISS?`

segments.voice: First, the line. In every single thing you do, Marcus writes, stop and ask yourself: is death terrible because it takes this away from me? That's the whole entry. Second, the test. Marcus is pointing the question at his own fear of dying. Much of what fills an hour isn't something we'd miss. If death is frightening because it would take away this errand, this complaint, this scroll, then the fear is smaller than it seemed. Third, the second edge. But the question cuts the other way too. If you look at what you're doing and the honest answer is, no, I wouldn't miss this, then why does so much of the day go to it? The question that loosens the fear of death also sorts the hours of a life. Some things pass the test easily. A long talk at the kitchen table. The evening walk. The work that matters to you. Fourth, not contempt. Marcus isn't saying ordinary life is worthless. A few entries earlier, he told himself to be content with what is given now. Towels still need folding. The point isn't to despise the errand. It's to see it at its real size, so it doesn't carry more weight than it should, either in your fears or in your hours. And Marcus leaves it as he found it: a question, asked again in every act.
screen: `STOP AND ASK, IN EVERY ACT.` · `THE FEAR SHRINKS TO SIZE.` · `THE QUESTION SORTS THE DAY.` · `NOT CONTEMPT: REAL SIZE.` · then, large: `IS IT THIS?`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Pick one ordinary task from today: something you did, or something still waiting for you. Look at it honestly. Ask Marcus's question: is this what I'd miss? Notice the answer. If it's no, notice what that does to the task. Maybe it gets lighter. Maybe it gets shorter. If it's yes, notice that too, and let it be precious. The bell holds the time.
Second edge. Marcus's question about death cuts both ways: it loosens the fear, and it sorts which hours are worth the day. Today's word.
Your line: is it this. Ask it three times today, in the middle of three ordinary tasks, and see what the answers sort. Day six hundred eighteen.

619.title: Let no one say it truly
619.hook: let no one be able to say truly that you aren't simple or good (Meditations 10.32)
619.howItsDone: People who use this passage often answer criticism by first asking whether it's true, and if any part is, by quietly changing that part rather than arguing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: second edge Your line was is it this. What did your three answers sort? Day six hundred nineteen.

Someone says something about you behind your back. Selfish, they say, or fake, or lazy. It stings, and it's easy to end up arguing with them in your head, in the shower, on the drive. But there's a quieter question underneath the sting: is it true? Marcus doesn't tell himself to stop people from talking. He tells himself something harder, and much more in his control. Today: two questions.
screen: `SAID BEHIND YOUR BACK.` → `ARGUING IN THE SHOWER.` → `LET NO ONE SAY IT TRULY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Let no one be able to say truthfully of you, Marcus writes, that you are not simple, or not good. Let anyone who thinks that of you be a liar. Second, the shift. He isn't trying to control what people say. People will say what they say. He's trying to control whether it's true. You can't stop the rumor. You can make it false. Third, it's in your power. All of this, he writes, is up to you. Who can stop you from being good and simple? No one. Other people can mislabel you, but they can't make the label stick to the person you actually are. Fourth, the test it gives. This turns criticism into something useful. When a remark lands, there are two questions. Is it true? If it isn't, it's their mistake, and you can let it go. If it is, even a little, then you've just been handed a free piece of information, and the work is to make it false, starting today. Either way, the energy goes into living, not into defending. And notice the two words he picks again: simple and good, the same pair book ten opened with, when he asked his soul whether it would ever be good and simple. A few pages later, he's still working on it.
screen: `LET THEM BE WRONG ABOUT YOU.` · `YOU CAN'T STOP THE RUMOR.` · `WHO CAN STOP YOU BEING GOOD?` · `TRUE? THEN MAKE IT FALSE.` · then, large: `LET IT BE FALSE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one criticism you've heard about yourself, or one you're afraid of. Hold it up to the light. Is there any truth in it? Be honest, and gentle. If there's none, set it down. If there's some, picture one act today that would make it false: the generous thing for selfish, the plain thing for fake, the finished thing for lazy. See yourself doing it. The bell holds the time.
Two questions. Marcus's test for criticism: is it true, and if so, what will you do to make it false. Today's word.
Your line: let it be false. Pick one criticism, fair or unfair, and act today so that it isn't true. Day six hundred nineteen.

620.title: Glad at your going
620.hook: no one is so lucky that no one will be glad at their death, not even Marcus (Meditations 10.36)
620.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use this passage to loosen the sense of being indispensable, picturing life going on without them while resolving to stay kind to everyone around them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two questions. Your line was let it be false. Which criticism did you make false today? Day six hundred twenty.

The last day at a job: the cake, the card, the kind speeches. And somewhere in the room, someone quietly relieved you're going. Maybe you never knew, and maybe that was for the best. Marcus, emperor of Rome, writes in book ten that it would be the same at his own death: someone standing by would be glad. Not because he was cruel. Just because that's how people are. Today: schoolmaster.
screen: `THE LAST DAY AT A JOB.` → `SOMEONE QUIETLY RELIEVED.` → `GLAD AT YOUR GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. No one is so fortunate, Marcus writes, that when they're dying there won't be some standing by who welcome what's happening. Second, even the good. Suppose the person was good and wise. Won't someone still say under their breath: at last we can breathe again, free of this schoolmaster? He was never harsh with any of us, but I always felt him quietly judging us. That, Marcus says, is what's said of a good man. Third, and me? Then he turns it on himself. In my case, he says, there are many more reasons people would be glad to be rid of me. Even the companions he has worked for, prayed for and cared for, he writes, will want him gone, hoping to gain something by it. It's humbling, written by a man who ruled the Roman world. Fourth, how to hold it. The point isn't bitterness. Marcus says: don't, for this reason, go away less kindly disposed toward them. Keep your own character: friendly, well-meaning, gentle. Let go easily, he says, not as if you were being torn away. So the thought is a lightness, not a wound. You aren't the center of everyone's world, even if you're good, and that's a kind of relief. If even the gentle schoolmaster can be resented, anyone can. Hold your importance lightly, and keep being kind.

A family dinner with your chair empty. Notice whatever comes: maybe a sting, maybe something lighter. Not everything rests on you. Breathe out a little of that weight. Then picture going back in, as kind as ever. The bell holds the time.

621.title: My own fruit
621.hook: the rational soul sees itself, shapes itself, and gathers its own fruit (Meditations 11.1)
621.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations end the day with a short, honest look at themselves, naming one good thing they grew and one thing to shape differently tomorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: schoolmaster. Your line was lightly. Where did you carry your importance lightly? Day six hundred twenty-one.

An apple tree grows an apple, and someone else eats it. A cow makes milk, and someone else drinks it. A vine grows grapes for somebody's table. Plants and animals, Marcus says, bear fruit that others enjoy. Book eleven of the Meditations opens with Marcus noticing that there's one kind of fruit that's different, one harvest that stays with the one who grows it. Today, as book eleven begins: my own fruit.
screen: `AN APPLE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `BOOK ELEVEN OPENS.` → `MY OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: First, the mirror. Marcus lists what the reasoning soul can do. It sees itself. It examines itself. It shapes itself into whatever it chooses. No plant can look at itself and decide to grow differently. We can. Second, the fruit. The fruit it bears, he says, it gathers for itself. A tree's fruit and an animal's yield are enjoyed by others. But the fruit of a well-lived life, steadiness, kindness, clear sight, belongs to the one who grew it. You don't have to wait for someone else to taste it. Third, whole at every point. Then a striking thought. A dance or a play, Marcus says, is left incomplete if it's cut off partway. But the soul reaches its own end wherever life stops. Each act done well is whole in itself, so at any moment it can say: I have what is my own. Fourth, the wide view. The soul, he goes on, ranges over the whole universe and the emptiness around it, stretches into endless time, and sees that those who come after us will see nothing new. A person of forty, he adds, with any understanding at all, has in a sense seen everything that has been and will be. He means the same patterns keep coming round. And the point holds closer to home. Look honestly at yourself, and the harvest is already yours.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. For a minute, look at yourself honestly, the way you'd look at a friend you love. Not judging, just seeing. What did you grow this week? Patience in one place? A kept promise? A kind word at the right time? Name one fruit. Don't wait for anyone else to notice it. Gather it yourself. Then notice one thing you'd like to shape differently, and simply set the intention. The bell holds the time.

622.title: Already rewarded
622.hook: have I done something for the common good? then I've been rewarded (Meditations 11.4)
622.howItsDone: People who take this note seriously often do small, unannounced things for shared spaces and neighbors, and treat the doing itself as the point rather than waiting for thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: my own fruit. Your line was gather your own harvest. What did you grow, and did you gather it? Day six hundred twenty-two.

Somewhere in most of us there's a receipt book. Drove her to the airport: one slip. Covered his shift: another. Remembered the birthday, listened for an hour on the phone, lent the ladder and got it back with a dent. Nobody asked us to keep it. We keep it anyway, and every slip says the same thing underneath: you owe me. Marcus wrote a short note in book eleven that closes the book before the first slip is written. Today: already rewarded.
screen: `A RECEIPT BOOK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `EVERY SLIP SAYS: YOU OWE ME.` → `ALREADY REWARDED.`

segments.voice: First, the note. Have I done something for the common good? Marcus asks. Then I've been rewarded. Keep this always at hand, he adds, and never stop. Second, why it's already paid. Back in book nine he put it sharply: wanting a return for a kindness is like an eye demanding a fee for seeing, or feet for walking. Seeing is what an eye is for. For Marcus, working with and for others is what a person is for, so the doing is the payment. Third, one letter. In book seven he plays on two Greek words that differ by a single letter. Melos means a limb, like an arm or a hand. Meros means a part, a piece, like one brick in a pile. If you think of yourself as only a part of humankind, he says, you don't yet love people from the heart. You do good because it's proper, as a duty. Think of yourself as a limb of the one body, and doing good becomes doing good to yourself. A hand doesn't send the arm an invoice. Fourth, why it's freeing. If the reward is in the doing, you can't be cheated out of it. No one can ignore you out of it. You don't need to keep the account, because it's settled the moment you act. That doesn't make thanks bad. Thanks is welcome. It just means you aren't waiting for it.

Now picture yourself not as a separate piece, but as one hand on a body that includes that person too. Let the slip go, just for this sit. Then think of one small thing you could do for the common good today, something shared: a cleared table, a refilled coffee pot, a question answered for a stranger. The bell holds the time.

623.title: Kind to everyone
623.hook: if someone despises me, that's theirs; mine is to be kind to all (Meditations 11.13)
623.howItsDone: People who draw on this passage often separate another person's dislike from their own conduct, checking whether they've given real cause, and then offering ordinary kindness regardless.

segments.voice: Yesterday: already rewarded. Your line was no invoice. Which quiet good did you do, and did the account stay closed? Day six hundred twenty-three, the end of a week.

There's someone who doesn't like you. Maybe a relative, a neighbor, a coworker who rolls their eyes when you talk. It's tempting to make it a project: win them over, or dislike them right back, or at least make sure everyone knows who started it. Marcus asks it plainly in book eleven: does someone despise me? Then he splits the problem neatly in two, and keeps only one half. Today: Phocion.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO DOESN'T LIKE YOU.` → `WIN THEM, OR DISLIKE THEM BACK?` → `KIND TO EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: First, the split. Does someone despise me? Marcus writes. That's for them to see to. Mine is to make sure I'm not found doing or saying anything that deserves contempt. Does someone hate me? Their concern. Mine is to be gentle and kind toward everyone, this person included. Second, ready to show them. He adds that he'll be ready to show that very person where they've gone wrong, not by scolding, and not by making a show of his own patience, but nobly and honestly. Third, Phocion. He gives an example: like the great Phocion, unless Phocion was only pretending. Phocion was an Athenian general condemned to death by his own city. Plutarch tells that before he died, someone asked whether he had a message for his son, and he said to tell him to bear no grudge against the Athenians. Marcus admires it, then adds a dry footnote: unless it was an act. Fourth, the week, looking back. As on a mountain. Is it this. Let it be false. Lightly. My own fruit. No invoice. And now, theirs, and mine. Several of them draw a line between what belongs to others and what belongs to you, and put your effort on your own side of it. Their opinion is theirs. Your kindness is yours.
screen: `THEIR CONTEMPT IS THEIRS.` · `MINE: BE KIND TO EVERYONE.` · `PHOCION: NO GRUDGE.` · `A WEEK OF DRAWING THE LINE.` · then, large: `THEIRS, AND MINE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture someone who dislikes you. See their face. Notice what rises. Now, in your mind, divide the space between you. On their side: their opinion of you. Leave it there. On your side: your own words and actions. Ask: is there anything I did that deserves their contempt? If so, note it. Then choose one small kindness you could offer them, plainly, with no show. The bell holds the time.
Phocion. The Athenian general condemned by his own city, who asked that his son bear no grudge against the Athenians. Today's word.
